# Endotoxins

Toxins closely associated with the living cytoplasm or cell wall of certain microorganisms, which do not readily diffuse into the culture medium, but are released upon lysis of the cells.

Numerous reports, including recent work, claim that “autoclaving cannot eliminate endotoxin”^{11} or “endotoxin is not reliably destroyed by disinfection, steam sterilization processes, or ethylene oxide sterilization,”^{12} without providing evidence or references.^{13}^{,}^{14}

In other instances, the statement about endotoxin inactivation appears in the context of a particular endpoint (e.g., a limit in EU/mL for a particular device). In one experiment, the authors described test results—“after 90 min, endotoxins treated with a 50% steam saturation ratio were not inactivated (LRV [Log Reduction Value] of 1.37 ± 0.30)”—in which detectable endotoxin was reduced by 1.37 logs (~95%) accompanied by a statement that endotoxin was not inactivated, as the result did not meet the desired endpoint of the study (i.e., a 3-log reduction).^{15} Clearly, describing whether a particular process is effective for inactivating endotoxin in a pass/fail manner is problematic because the extent of endotoxin reduction varies by the extent of treatment and the acceptance criteria for endotoxin reduction varies according to the purpose of the test.
